name: ufw
description: Uncomplicated Firewall: a friendly front end to nftables/iptables for managing Linux firewall rules.

flags.description: Activate / deactivate the firewall (persists across reboots).
Rules and default policies in readable form.
Permit a port, e.g. allow 22/tcp or allow 80,443/tcp.
Set the default policy (deny incoming is the safe baseline).

examples.command: sudo ufw allow OpenSSH && sudo ufw enable
examples.explanation: THE safe activation sequence: allow SSH FIRST, then enable — otherwise enabling ufw on a remote server cuts your connection.

examples.output:
Status: active
Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing)
To         Action      From
22/tcp     LIMIT IN    Anywhere
80,443/tcp ALLOW IN    Anywhere
examples.explanation: Deny-by-default with explicit exceptions: SSH (rate-limited) and web ports. This is the shape of a healthy server firewall.

examples.command: sudo ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/24 to any port 5432
examples.explanation: Allows PostgreSQL access ONLY from the internal network — never from the whole internet.
Removes a rule that is no longer needed.

about: ufw translates simple rules into nftables (older: iptables). Default policies matter most: deny incoming, allow outgoing is the standard starting point. Rules are evaluated top-down; the first match wins, so ordering matters. ufw persists its state across reboots automatically once enabled.
useCases: Restricting database/service ports to internal networks.
mistakes: Enabling ufw before allowing SSH — you lock yourself out of a remote server.
Assuming ufw is active by default — it is inactive until enabled.
warnings: On cloud providers (AWS/GCP/Azure), security groups filter traffic BEFORE ufw; both layers must allow the port.
distroNotes: Preinstalled on Ubuntu; available in most distro repositories. RHEL-family commonly uses firewalld (firewall-cmd) instead.
